A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Data Caricatures study. Their main text, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original corpus measurements, human judgments of AAL texts, linguistic-feature and lyric-overlap analyses, and experiments evaluating 16 automated filters.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds cross-corpus duplication measurements, broader feature and lyric-overlap analyses, and classifier examples.

M1.justification: The demographic-alignment classifier, CGEdit feature detector, C4 blocklist, human-rating scheme, and normalized filter-scoring procedures are retained. V2 extends analyses of their outputs without revising the underlying models or procedures.

E1.justification: Both versions cover the same 12 pretraining corpora and the same dialogue, social-media, and song-lyric sources used for filter evaluation. The additional appendix analyses reuse these corpora without introducing another language, population, or input domain.

E2.justification: The same 16 automated filters participate in the corresponding comparisons, and FineWeb-Edu remains the corpus baseline. V1 Table 9 and v2 Table 11 describe the same filter set.

E3.justification: New analyses introduce sampling protocols: up to 50,000 documents per corpus for feature analysis and 50% samples for lyric overlap, with all extracted OpenWebText AAL texts used instead. Existing corpus-extraction budgets, annotation collection, and filter-evaluation settings remain substantially unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 substantially expands diagnostic analysis through cross-corpus document overlap (Section 4.2), classifier examples illustrating identification failures (Appendix F), and corpus-wide feature and lyric-overlap analyses (Appendices G and I). The earlier vocabulary-overlap, non-AAL annotation, and source-category analyses are retained under new appendix labels.

E5.justification: Both versions retain 99% confidence intervals, two-tailed t-tests, the same significance threshold, weighted human-judgment estimates, and Cohen's kappa/Spearman agreement reporting. Changed support entries in Table 7 do not establish additional annotation runs or a revised statistical procedure.

E6.justification: V2 adds the finding that 17% of analyzed AAL documents occur in another corpus, corpus-wide feature and lyric distributions, classifier examples, and full Likert-rating distributions. Table 1 changes OpenWebText from 2,684 AAL documents (0.03%) to 858 (0.01%). Table 7 changes reported support from 40.3/13.7 to 121/41 while retaining the agreement coefficients; the principal filter findings and C4 judgment percentages remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Neither version introduces original theoretical propositions or proofs. The existing classifier-selection criteria and mathematical descriptions of filter-score normalization are substantively unchanged.

C1.justification: V2 adds shared AAL documents across corpora to its concluding claims and explicitly frames inappropriate or stereotypical content in the abstract as perceived judgments. The central claims about underrepresentation, misrepresentation, and differential filtering remain intact.

C2.justification: V2 interprets cross-corpus duplication as limited diversity and suggests spurious token features explain declining human confirmation at higher classifier probabilities. The discussion expands implications for feature-specific language understanding. The principal limitations concerning classifier transfer and annotator representativeness remain unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-availability link, identifies UpSetPlot, clarifies hash-ordered sampling to the 250 GB threshold, and documents sampling for the new analyses. It also removes Table 5's statement about matching text lengths where possible; the PDFs do not establish a corresponding change to the collected data.

R1.justification: V2 adds supporting references concerning reward-model bias, linguistic perceptions, demographics, chatbot trust, and language-technology accessibility, including Mire et al. (2025), Labov et al. (2011), and Basoah et al. (2025). Its central positioning around pretraining data as a source of AAL bias is retained.

P1.justification: V2 adds research-question overview paragraphs and acknowledgments, expands the discussion, clarifies sampling prose, and moves annotation rationale from Appendix D.4 into Section 5.1. The three-question organization and most existing exposition remain recognizable.

P2.justification: V2 adds an intersection plot, corpus-wide feature and lyric charts, and two classifier-example tables. It substantially redesigns the annotation summary into a full Likert-distribution display and updates colors, axis labels, captions, and placement of retained figures and tables.

improvement.justification: The new corpus-wide checks strengthen support for feature and lyric patterns that v1 examined mainly in C4, while duplication analysis adds evidence about diversity across corpora. Classifier examples, fuller rating displays, clearer sampling descriptions, and code information improve transparency. These gains remain limited by the unresolved low human confirmation of classifier-selected texts in Table 2 and the retained annotation limitations.
